claim: FBXL19 is a CpG island-binding protein in mouse embryonic stem (ES) cells
source: Here, we identify FBXL19 as a CpG island-binding protein in mouse embryonic stem (ES) cells
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data showing FBXL19 enrichment at CpG islands (Figure 1D-F) and experimental validation

claim: FBXL19 associates with the CDK-Mediator complex
source: Here, we identify FBXL19 as a CpG island-binding protein in mouse embryonic stem (ES) cells and show that it associates with the CDK-Mediator complex.
evidence: Supported by affinity purification mass spectrometry (AP-MS) data (Figure 2A) and co-immunoprecipitation experiments

claim: FBXL19 recruits CDK-Mediator to CpG island-associated promoters of non-transcribed developmental genes
source: We discover that FBXL19 recruits CDK-Mediator to CpG island-associated promoters of non-transcribed developmental genes to prime these genes for activation during cell lineage commitment.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data showing reduced CDK8 occupancy at developmental gene promoters in FBXL19ΔCXXC cells (Figure 4) and TetO array recruitment experiments (Figure 3)

claim: FBXL19 primes developmental genes for activation during cell lineage commitment
source: We discover that FBXL19 recruits CDK-Mediator to CpG island-associated promoters of non-transcribed developmental genes to prime these genes for activation during cell lineage commitment.
evidence: Supported by 4sU RNA-seq data showing impaired gene activation during differentiation in FBXL19ΔCXXC cells (Figure 6)

claim: Recognition of CpG islands by FBXL19 is essential for mouse development
source: We further show that recognition of CpG islands by FBXL19 is essential for mouse development.
evidence: Supported by embryonic lethality observed in Fbxl19ΔCXXC homozygous mice (Figure 8)

claim: FBXL19 is predominantly found in the nucleus
source: This revealed that FBXL19 was almost exclusively nuclear (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescent staining (Figure 1B) and subcellular fractionation (Figure 1C)

claim: FBXL19 associates with chromatin
source: Importantly, FBXL19 was found not only in the soluble nuclear extract but also in the insoluble nuclear pellet, which contains chromatin-bound factors (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by subcellular fractionation showing FBXL19 in the insoluble nuclear pellet

claim: FBXL19 binds to CpG islands in a manner highly similar to KDM2A and KDM2B
source: We observed that FBXL19 ChIP-seq signal at NMIs was highly similar to that of KDM2A and KDM2B (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data comparing FBXL19, KDM2A, and KDM2B binding patterns

claim: FBXL19 ChIP-seq signal correlates with the density of non-methylated CpG dinucleotides in NMIs
source: Furthermore, FBXL19 ChIP-seq signal correlated well with the density of non-methylated CpG dinucleotides in NMIs, similarly to KDM2A and KDM2B, (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between FBXL19 ChIP-seq and BioCAP signal

claim: Almost all FBXL19-occupied sites fall within NMIs
source: and almost all FBXL19-occupied sites fell within NMIs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by overlap analysis between FBXL19 peaks and NMIs

claim: The association of FBXL19 with CpG islands is dependent on its ZF-CxxC domain
source: This revealed a near complete loss of FBXL19 binding to chromatin when the ZF-CxxC domain was deleted and a slightly less dramatic effect in the K49A mutant (Figure 1H,I, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data comparing wild-type and mutant FBXL19

claim: FBXL19 interacts with SKP1
source: This revealed that FBXL19 interacts with SKP1, a known F-box-binding protein that also associates with KDM2A and KDM2B (Bai et al., 1996; Farcas et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by AP-MS data (Figure 2A) and Western blot validation

claim: FBXL19 interacts with the nuclear proteasome activator PSME3
source: This revealed that FBXL19 interacts with SKP1, a known F-box-binding protein that also associates with KDM2A and KDM2B (Bai et al., 1996; Farcas et al., 2012), and the nuclear proteasome activator PSME3 (Wójcik et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by AP-MS data (Figure 2A)

claim: FBXL19 interacts with multiple subunits of the Mediator complex in a sub-stoichiometric manner
source: Interestingly, we also identified multiple subunits of the Mediator complex that appeared to interact with FBXL19 in a sub-stoichiometric manner (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by AP-MS data showing Mediator subunits with low emPAI values

claim: FBXL19 purification identified subunits of the kinase-containing Mediator complex (CDK-Mediator), but not MED26 or RNAPolII
source: Interestingly, our FBXL19 purification identified subunits of the kinase-containing Mediator complex (CDK-Mediator), but not MED26 or RNAPolII (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by AP-MS data showing presence of CDK-Mediator subunits and absence of MED26 and RNAPolII

claim: FBXL19 interacts preferentially with CDK-Mediator
source: This suggests that FBXL19 interacts preferentially with CDK-Mediator, however, we cannot exclude the possibly it may also interact with MED26-Mediator.
evidence: Inferred from AP-MS data showing CDK-Mediator subunits but not MED26

claim: FBXL19 is likely able to interact with both CDK8- and CDK19-containing Mediator complexes
source: Therefore, it is likely that FBXL19 is able to interact with both CDK8- and CDK19-containing Mediator complexes.
evidence: Inferred from mass spectrometry data showing peptides common between CDK8 and CDK19

claim: The association of FBXL19 with CDK-Mediator is sub-stoichiometric and likely weak
source: This is in agreement with our mass spectrometry analysis, which indicated that the association of FBXL19 with CDK-Mediator is sub-stoichiometric, and suggests that this interaction is likely weak, as opposed to stable, inside cells.
evidence: Inferred from failure to detect FBXL19 in reciprocal immunopurifications and low emPAI values in AP-MS

claim: FBXL19 relies on its F-box domain for association with CDK-Mediator
source: Intact FBXL19 and a version with the ZF-CxxC domain removed interacted with CDK-Mediator, whereas removing the F-box domain resulted in a loss of this interaction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by affinity purification experiments with FBXL19 truncation mutants

claim: FBXL19 does not interact with RNF20/40 E3 ubiquitin ligase in unbiased biochemical purification
source: In our unbiased biochemical purification of FBXL19, we did not identify an interaction with RNF20/40 by AP-MS or by western blot analysis (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by absence of RNF20/40 in AP-MS data and Western blot validation

claim: There is no relationship between the ability of FBXL19 to associate with CpG islands and the levels of H2BK120ub1
source: Furthermore, we failed to observe any relationship between the ability of FBXL19 to associate with CpG islands and the levels of H2BK120ub1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis of H2BK120ub1 levels in wild-type and FBXL19ΔCXXC cells

claim: FBXL19 does not function as a SCF substrate selector for CDK-Mediator
source: Based on these observations, we conclude that FBXL19 does not function as a SCF substrate selector for CDK-Mediator.
evidence: Inferred from absence of CUL1 and RBX1/2 in FBXL19 purifications and lack of effect on CDK-Mediator protein levels

claim: FBXL19 is sufficient to recruit CDK-Mediator to chromatin
source: Consistent with our biochemical observations (Figure 2), when we examined the binding of CDK8 and MED12 over the TetO array, we observed an enrichment in the TetR-FBXL19 line.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data showing CDK8 and MED12 enrichment at TetO array in TetR-FBXL19 cells

claim: FBXL19 may be sufficient to recruit a holo-CDK-Mediator complex
source: Furthermore, binding of MED4, which is part of the core Mediator complex, was also evident at the TetO array (Figure 3B). This suggests that FBXL19 may be sufficient to recruit a holo-CDK-Mediator complex
evidence: Inferred from ChIP-qPCR data showing enrichment of both CDK-Mediator and core Mediator subunits at TetO array

claim: TetR-KDM2A and TetR-KDM2B do not lead to CDK8 recruitment
source: Importantly, stable expression of TetR-KDM2A and TetR-KDM2B did not lead to CDK8 recruitment, indicating that this activity is unique to FBXL19 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data showing lack of CDK8 enrichment at TetO array in TetR-KDM2A and TetR-KDM2B cells

claim: CDK8 occupancy is not restricted to CpG islands
source: Unlike FBXL19, CDK8 occupancy was not restricted to CpG islands (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), with only 67.5% of CDK8 peaks overlapping with NMIs
evidence: Supported by CDK8 ChIP-seq data and overlap analysis with NMIs

claim: CDK8 binding shows a limited correlation with BioCAP signal
source: with only 67.5% of CDK8 peaks overlapping with NMIs and CDK8 binding showing a limited correlation with BioCAP signal (Spearman correlation – 0.48, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between CDK8 ChIP-seq and BioCAP signal

claim: 89.4% of FBXL19 peaks overlap with CDK8 peaks and NMIs
source: Interestingly, however, we observed enrichment of CDK8 at FBXL19 peaks (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) with 89.4% of FBXL19 peaks overlapping with CDK8 peaks and NMIs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: Supported by overlap analysis between FBXL19 peaks, CDK8 peaks, and NMIs

claim: Removal of the ZF-CxxC domain of FBXL19 leads to some reductions in FBXL19 protein levels
source: Following removal of the ZF-CxxC domain of FBXL19, we observed some reductions in FBXL19 protein levels (Figure 4B)
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis showing reduced FBXL19 protein in FBXL19ΔCXXC cells

claim: CDK8 levels are unaffected by removal of the ZF-CxxC domain of FBXL19
source: but importantly CDK8 levels were unaffected (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis showing unchanged CDK8 protein levels in FBXL19ΔCXXC cells

claim: FBXL19 is not the central determinant driving CDK8 recruitment to most of its binding sites in the genome
source: Genome-wide profiling of CDK8 in Fbxll19ΔCXXC ES cells did not reveal widespread alterations in CDK8 binding (Figure 4C left and Figure 4—figure supplement 1H), indicating that FBXL19 is not the central determinant driving CDK8 recruitment to most of its binding sites in the genome.
evidence: Supported by CDK8 ChIP-seq data showing limited genome-wide changes in FBXL19ΔCXXC cells

claim: A subset of CDK8 target sites display significant alteration in CDK8 occupancy in FBXL19ΔCXXC cells
source: Intriguingly, however, a more detailed site-specific analysis revealed a subset of CDK8 target sites that displayed significant alteration in CDK8 occupancy (Figure 4C,D, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by differential binding analysis of CDK8 ChIP-seq data

claim: The majority of CDK8 sites affected by FBXL19 deletion showed reduced CDK8 binding (n = 783)
source: In keeping with a potential role for FBXL19 in CDK8 recruitment, the majority of the affected sites showed reduced CDK8 binding (n = 783) (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by differential binding analysis showing 783 sites with reduced CDK8 binding

claim: Sites with reduced CDK8 occupancy in Fbxll19ΔCXXC ES cells tend to coincide with broad regions of CDK8 enrichment
source: Upon closer examination of sites with reduced CDK8 occupancy in Fbxll19ΔCXXC ES cells, we discovered that they tended to coincide with broad regions of CDK8 enrichment (Figure 4E,F)
evidence: Supported by analysis of CDK8 peak size at differential sites

claim: Sites with reduced CDK8 occupancy are distinct from super-enhancers
source: However, a comparison of these sites to the location of super-enhancers in mouse ES cells indicated that these were distinct (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by overlap analysis between CDK8 differential sites and super-enhancers

claim: Sites displaying reduction in CDK8 occupancy coincide with broad regions of non-methylated DNA
source: Instead, sites displaying reduction in CDK8 occupancy coincided with broad regions of non-methylated DNA (Figure 4D,H, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1H)
evidence: Supported by BioCAP signal analysis at CDK8 differential sites

claim: Sites with reduced CDK8 occupancy tend to be associated with gene promoters
source: tended to be associated with gene promoters (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I)
evidence: Supported by overlap analysis between CDK8 differential sites and transcription start sites

claim: Sites with reduced CDK8 occupancy have elevated levels of FBXL19
source: and had elevated levels of FBXL19 (Figure 4I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1H,I,J).
evidence: Supported by FBXL19 ChIP-seq signal analysis at CDK8 differential sites

claim: Genes with reduced CDK8 levels at their promoters in Fbxl19ΔCXXC ES cells are strongly enriched for developmental processes
source: Interestingly, this revealed that these genes were strongly enriched for developmental processes (Figure 5A)
evidence: Supported by gene ontology analysis of genes associated with reduced CDK8 binding

claim: Broad CpG islands are an evolutionary conserved feature of developmentally regulated genes
source: in agreement with our previous discovery that broad CpG islands are an evolutionary conserved feature of developmentally regulated genes (Long et al., 2013b).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: Genes associated with reduced CDK8 binding are expressed at significantly lower levels than most other genes in ES cells
source: Importantly, the genes that exhibited reductions in CDK8 binding in Fbxl19ΔCXXC cells were expressed at significantly lower levels than most other genes in ES cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq expression analysis of genes associated with differential CDK8 binding

claim: Sites that rely on FBXL19 for normal CDK8 binding are enriched for H3K27me3
source: We found that these regions are enriched for H3K27me3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by H3K27me3 ChIP-seq analysis at CDK8 differential sites

claim: Sites that rely on FBXL19 for normal CDK8 binding have elevated H3K4me3 compared to other H3K27me3-modified sites that lack CDK8
source: and have elevated H3K4me3 compared to other H3K27me3-modified sites that lack CDK8 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by H3K4me3 ChIP-seq analysis at H3K27me3 peaks with and without CDK8

claim: Sites that rely on FBXL19 for normal CDK8 binding correspond to silent developmental gene promoters that are bivalent
source: Therefore, sites that rely on FBXL19 for normal CDK8 binding and correspond to silent developmental gene promoters are also bivalent.
evidence: Inferred from H3K27me3 and H3K4me3 ChIP-seq data at CDK8 differential sites

claim: Genes that rely on FBXL19 for appropriate CDK8 binding in the ES cell state can become transcriptionally activated during stem cell lineage commitment
source: This clearly demonstrated that the genes which rely on FBXL19 for appropriate CDK8 binding in the ES cell state can become transcriptionally activated during stem cell lineage commitment (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by 4sU RNA-seq data comparing ES cells and RA-treated cells

claim: CDK8 occupancy is in general linked to gene activity
source: We observed that CDK8 occupancy was in general linked to gene activity (Figure 5E), in agreement with previous reports (Alarcón et al., 2009; Bancerek et al., 2013; Donner et al., 2010; Donner et al., 2007; Fryer et al., 2004; Galbraith et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by CDK8 ChIP-seq analysis at genes with different expression levels and citations to previous studies

claim: At FBXL19-bound gene promoters, CDK8 occupancy is similar in both lowly and highly expressed subsets of genes
source: However, at FBXL19-bound gene promoters, CDK8 occupancy was similar in both the lowly and highly expressed subsets of genes (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by CDK8 ChIP-seq analysis at FBXL19-bound genes with different expression levels

claim: CDK8 occupancy at promoters of lowly expressed genes is reduced in Fbxl19ΔCXXC ES cells
source: Importantly, CDK8 occupancy at promoters of lowly expressed genes was reduced in Fbxl19ΔCXXC ES cells (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by differential CDK8 binding analysis at genes with different expression levels

claim: CDK8 is enriched at promoters of inactive or lowly expressed genes in ES cells and its binding is dependent on recognition of CpG islands by FBXL19
source: Therefore, these observations reveal that CDK8 is enriched at promoters of inactive or lowly expressed genes in ES cells and its binding is dependent on recognition of CpG islands by FBXL19.
evidence: Inferred from CDK8 ChIP-seq and differential binding analysis at genes with different expression levels

claim: No significant differences in expression of developmental genes are observed in wild-type Fbxl19fl/fl and Fbxl19ΔCXXC ES cells where these genes are silent
source: We observed no significant differences in the expression of these genes in wild-type Fbxl19fl/fl and Fbxl19ΔCXXC ES cells where these genes are silent.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data comparing gene expression in wild-type and FBXL19ΔCXXC ES cells

claim: Following RA treatment, Fbxl19ΔCXXC cells fail to induce developmental genes appropriately
source: Strikingly, however, following RA treatment, Fbxl19ΔCXXC cells failed to induce these genes appropriately (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data comparing gene expression in wild-type and FBXL19ΔCXXC cells after RA treatment

claim: Developmental genes are not appropriately induced during embryoid body differentiation of Fbxl19ΔCXXC ES cells
source: Similarly, developmental genes were not appropriately induced during embryoid body differentiation of Fbxl19ΔCXXC ES cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data during embryoid body differentiation time course

claim: FBXL19 is required for the appropriate activation of developmental gene expression during cell lineage commitment
source: Importantly, this demonstrates that FBXL19 is required for the appropriate activation of developmental gene expression during cell lineage commitment.
evidence: Inferred from RT-qPCR and 4sU RNA-seq data showing impaired gene activation in FBXL19ΔCXXC cells during differentiation

claim: Genes that are not appropriately activated in FBXL19ΔCXXC cells are associated with developmental processes
source: GO analysis revealed that the set of genes that were not appropriately activated were associated with genes involved in developmental processes (Figure 6D and Figure 6—source data 1)
evidence: Supported by gene ontology analysis of down-regulated genes in FBXL19ΔCXXC cells after RA treatment

claim: Genes not appropriately induced in FBXL19ΔCXXC cells are lowly expressed in wild-type ES cells
source: Nevertheless, consistent with our analysis of FBXL19-dependent CDK8 occupancy at promoters of developmental genes (Figure 5B,C), genes not appropriately induced were lowly expressed in wild-type ES cells (Figure 6E)
evidence: Supported by expression analysis of differentially expressed genes in wild-type ES cells

claim: Genes not appropriately induced in FBXL19ΔCXXC cells tend to become activated following RA induction
source: and tended to become activated following RA induction (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by expression analysis comparing ES cells and RA-treated cells

claim: Genes not appropriately induced in FBXL19ΔCXXC cells exhibit a reduction in CDK8 binding in Fbxl19ΔCXXC ES cells
source: Importantly, these genes exhibited a reduction in CDK8 binding in Fbxl19ΔCXXC ES cells (Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: Supported by CDK8 ChIP-seq analysis at differentially expressed genes

claim: Treatment of Med13/13lfl/fl ES cells with OHT results in a loss of MED13 and MED13L protein
source: Treatment of the Med13/13lfl/fl ES cells with OHT resulted in a loss of MED13 and MED13L protein (MED13/13L KO) and reduced levels of the other subunits of the CDK-kinase module (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis showing loss of MED13/13L protein

claim: Removal of MED13/13L leads to reduced levels of other subunits of the CDK-kinase module
source: Treatment of the Med13/13lfl/fl ES cells with OHT resulted in a loss of MED13 and MED13L protein (MED13/13L KO) and reduced levels of the other subunits of the CDK-kinase module (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis showing reduced levels of CDK-kinase module subunits

claim: Removal of MED13/13L leads to a loss of CDK8 binding to chromatin
source: Importantly, removal of MED13/13L also led to a loss of CDK8 binding to chromatin (Figure 7C)
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data showing reduced CDK8 enrichment in MED13/13L KO cells

claim: Removal of MED13/13L does not have an appreciable effect on the expression of FBXL19 target genes in the ES cell state
source: but did not have an appreciable effect on the expression of FBXL19 target genes in the ES cell state (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data comparing gene expression in wild-type and MED13/13L KO ES cells

claim: Genes that rely on FBXL19 for activation during differentiation fail to appropriately induce in MED13/13L KO cells
source: Importantly, when we then analysed the expression of a series of genes that rely on FBXL19 for activation during differentiation (Figure 7D), we observed that these genes also failed to appropriately induce in MED13/13L KO cells (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data comparing gene expression in wild-type and MED13/13L KO cells after RA treatment

claim: FBXL19, via its association with CpG islands, recognizes a subset of silent developmental genes in ES cells to recruit the CDK-Mediator complex and prime these genes for future activation
source: Together this suggests that FBXL19, via its association with CpG islands, recognises a subset of silent developmental genes in ES cells in order to recruit the CDK-Mediator complex and prime these genes for future activation.
evidence: Inferred from combined data showing FBXL19-dependent CDK8 recruitment and requirement for both FBXL19 and MED13/13L for gene activation

claim: Removal of the ZF-CxxC domain of FBXL19 leads to embryonic lethality
source: From these crosses, we failed to obtain any viable Fbxl19ΔCXXC homozygous offspring, indicating that removal of the ZF-CxxC domain of FBXL19 leads to embryonic lethality (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by absence of viable homozygous offspring from genetic crosses

claim: Fbxl19ΔCXXC homozygous embryos are observed at normal Mendelian ratios until 10.5 days postcoitum (dpc)
source: We then investigated at which stage Fbxl19ΔCXXC homozygous embryos were affected and found homozygous embryos were observed at normal Mendelian ratios until 10.5 days postcoitum (dpc) (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by genotyping data from embryos at different developmental stages

claim: At 9.5 dpc, gross embryonic morphology of Fbxl19ΔCXXC homozygous embryos appears to be intact
source: At 9.5 dpc, gross embryonic morphology appeared to be intact but at 10.5 dpc (Figure 8B) the embryos exhibited a clear growth retardation
evidence: Supported by morphological examination of embryos at 9.5 dpc

claim: At 10.5 dpc, Fbxl19ΔCXXC homozygous embryos exhibit clear growth retardation and developmental defects
source: At 9.5 dpc, gross embryonic morphology appeared to be intact but at 10.5 dpc (Figure 8B) the embryos exhibited a clear growth retardation and showed, to varying extents, reduced elongation of the trunk, hypomorphic limb buds and cephalic region.
evidence: Supported by morphological examination of embryos at 10.5 dpc

claim: Fbxl19ΔCXXC homozygous embryos show defects in maxillary and mandibular components of first branchial arches
source: This included undeveloped facial mesenchyme, including defects in maxillary and mandibular components of first branchial arches (indicated by yellow and red arrows in Figure 8B, respectively)
evidence: Supported by morphological examination of embryos at 10.5 dpc

claim: Fbxl19ΔCXXC homozygous embryos show hypomorphic cardiac mesenchyme
source: and hypomorphic cardiac mesenchyme.
evidence: Supported by morphological examination of embryos at 10.5 dpc

claim: Some living Fbxl19ΔCXXC homozygous embryos are observed at 12.5 dpc but they are of similar size and external appearance to 10.5 dpc mutant embryos
source: Some living Fbxl19ΔCXXC homozygous embryos, characterized by a beating heart, were observed at 12.5 dpc but they were of similar size and external appearance to 10.5 dpc mutant embryos suggesting that normal development had ceased by this point.
evidence: Supported by morphological examination of embryos at 12.5 dpc

claim: FBXL19 and its ability to recognize CpG islands is essential for normal mouse embryonic development
source: Together our findings demonstrate that FBXL19, and its ability to recognize CpG islands, is essential for normal mouse embryonic development.
evidence: Inferred from embryonic lethality and developmental defects in Fbxl19ΔCXXC mice

claim: CpG dinucleotides are pervasively methylated in mammalian genomes
source: In mammalian genomes, CpG dinucleotides are pervasively methylated and this epigenetically maintained DNA modification is generally associated with transcriptional inhibition, playing a central role in silencing of repetitive and parasitic DNA elements (Klose and Bird, 2006; Schübeler, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature

claim: DNA methylation is generally associated with transcriptional inhibition
source: In mammalian genomes, CpG dinucleotides are pervasively methylated and this epigenetically maintained DNA modification is generally associated with transcriptional inhibition, playing a central role in silencing of repetitive and parasitic DNA elements (Klose and Bird, 2006; Schübeler, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature

claim: Most gene promoters are embedded in CpG islands which remain free of DNA methylation
source: Most gene promoters, however, are embedded in short elements with elevated CpG dinucleotide content, called CpG islands, which remain free of DNA methylation (Bird et al., 1985; Illingworth and Bird, 2009; Larsen et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature

claim: The ZF-CxxC domain can recognize CpG dinucleotides when they are non-methylated
source: Interestingly, mammalian cells have evolved a DNA-binding domain, called a ZF-CxxC domain, which can recognize CpG dinucleotides when they are non-methylated (Lee et al., 2001; Voo et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature

claim: ZF-CxxC domain-containing proteins have the capacity to recognize and bind CpG islands throughout the genome
source: This endows ZF-CxxC domain-containing proteins with the capacity to recognize and bind CpG islands throughout the genome (Blackledge et al., 2010; Thomson et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature

claim: There are 12 mammalian proteins encoding a ZF-CxxC domain
source: There are 12 mammalian proteins encoding a ZF-CxxC domain, most of which are found in large chromatin modifying complexes that post-translationally modify histone proteins to regulate gene expression from CpG islands (Long et al., 2013a).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature

claim: KDM2A is a JmjC-domain-containing histone lysine demethylase that removes H3K36me1/2 from CpG islands
source: KDM2A is a JmjC-domain-containing histone lysine demethylase that removes histone H3 lysine 36 mono- and di- methylation (H3K36me1/2) from CpG islands (Blackledge et al., 2010; Tsukada et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature

claim: H3K36me1/me2 is found throughout the genome and is thought to be repressive to gene transcription
source: Like DNA methylation, H3K36me1/me2 is found throughout the genome and is thought to be repressive to gene transcription (Carrozza et al., 2005; Keogh et al., 2005; Peters et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature

claim: KDM2A has two paralogues in vertebrates: KDM2B and FBXL19
source: Sequence-based homology searches revealed that KDM2A has two paralogues in vertebrates, KDM2B and FBXL19 (Katoh and Katoh, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature

claim: KDM2B binds to CpG islands and can function as a histone demethylase for H3K36me1/2
source: KDM2B, like KDM2A, binds to CpG islands and can function as a histone demethylase for H3K36me1/2 via its JmjC domain (Farcas et al., 2012; He et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature

claim: KDM2B physically associates with PRC1 to control how transcriptionally repressive polycomb chromatin domains form at a subset of CpG island-associated genes
source: However, unlike KDM2A, it physically associates with the polycomb repressive complex 1 (PRC1) to control how transcriptionally repressive polycomb chromatin domains form at a subset of CpG island-associated genes (Blackledge et al., 2014; Farcas et al., 2012; He et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature

claim: FBXL19 lacks a JmjC domain and does not have demethylase activity
source: Unlike KDM2A and KDM2B, it lacks a JmjC domain and, therefore, does not have demethylase activity (Long et al., 2013a).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature and domain architecture analysis

claim: Multicellular development relies on the formation of cell-type-specific gene expression programmes
source: Multicellular development relies on the formation of cell-type-specific gene expression programmes that support differentiation.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about development

claim: Individual Mediator subunits interact with DNA-binding transcription factors that recruit the Mediator complex to specific DNA sequences
source: Individual Mediator subunits have been shown to interact with DNA-binding transcription factors that recruit the Mediator complex to specific DNA sequences in regulatory elements and support gene expression (Black et al., 2006; Blazek et al., 2005; Fondell et al., 1996; Malik and Roeder, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature

claim: CDK8 and CDK19 share 77% amino acid identity (89% similarity)
source: CDK8 and its paralogue CDK19 share 77% amino acid identity (89% similarity) (Audetat et al., 2017; Galbraith et al., 2013; Sato et al., 2004; Tsutsui et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature

claim: MED13/13L physically links the CDK-kinase module to the core Mediator complex
source: We chose to inactivate MED13/13L as it has previously been shown to physically link the CDK-kinase module to the core Mediator complex and underpin the formation of a functional CDK-Mediator (Knuesel et al., 2009; Tsai et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature

claim: CDK-Mediator has been associated with gene repression
source: Historically, CDK-Mediator has been associated with gene repression (Akoulitchev et al., 2000; Chi et al., 2001; Elmlund et al., 2006; Hengartner et al., 1998; Knuesel et al., 2009; Pavri et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature

claim: Several reports support the idea that CDK-Mediator is also involved in gene activation
source: These observations are in line with several reports that support the idea that CDK-Mediator is also involved in gene activation (Alarcón et al., 2009; Donner et al., 2007; Hirst et al., 1999; Donner et al., 2010; Galbraith et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature

claim: CDK8 is required for appropriate re-induction of inducible genes following an initial activation stimulus in yeast and human systems
source: Our finding that FBXL19 can target CDK8 to gene promoters and that this is required to prime the expression of developmental genes during ES cell differentiation is conceptually reminiscent of recent work in yeast and human systems which suggested that CDK8 is required for appropriate re-induction of inducible genes following an initial activation stimulus (D'Urso et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature

claim: CDK8 associates with the promoters of inducible genes following initial activation, acting as a form of transcriptional memory
source: In this study, CDK8 was found to associate with the promoters of inducible genes following initial activation, even in the absence of appreciable ongoing gene transcription, thereby acting as a form of transcriptional memory (D'Urso et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature

claim: Many developmental genes are inactive in pluripotent mouse ES cells and only become expressed as cells commit to more differentiated lineages
source: In pluripotent mouse ES cells, many developmental genes are inactive and only become expressed as cells commit to more differentiated lineages (Boyer et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature

claim: A subset of poised but inactive developmental genes in ES cells are proposed to exist in a bivalent chromatin state characterized by co-occurrence of H3K4me and H3K27me
source: Previous work has identified a subset of poised but inactive developmental genes in ES cells that are proposed to exist in a bivalent chromatin state characterized by the co-occurrence of histone H3 lysine 4 and 27 methylation (H3K4/K27me) (Bernstein et al., 2006; Mikkelsen et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature

claim: FBW7 functions as an E3 ubiquitin ligase substrate selector for the MED13/13L subunit of CDK-Mediator
source: Previously, another F-box protein, FBW7, was shown to function as an E3 ubiquitin ligase substrate selector for the MED13/13L subunit of CDK-Mediator and to regulate its stability through proteasomal degradation (Davis et al., 2013).
